Robert Douglas
rob'ūrt dug'las
n. (Robert Douglas, 1594–1674, five times Moderator of the Scottish General Assembly, leader of the Resolutioners)
German Robert, bright fame; Douglas, from Gaelic dubh glas, dark water.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Robert Douglas was the most considerable churchman in Scotland for a generation. Chaplain to the Scots regiments in Germany under Gustavus Adolphus in his youth, minister of Edinburgh from 1641, he was chosen Moderator of the General Assembly five times, preached at the coronation of Charles II at Scone on 1 January 1651 — a sermon of blunt warning to the young king about the Covenant he was swearing — and led the Resolutioner party through the whole controversy. He was wrong about the Public Resolutions, and the dictionary says so in the entry on them. It also records what he did in 1662, when the king he had crowned offered him a bishopric: he refused it, was deprived of his Edinburgh charge, and spent his last twelve years as a nonconforming minister in a country parish, dying in 1674. The man who had argued that the Church might stretch a point for the sake of the king would not stretch one for the king's episcopacy. “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a moderator as the president of a meeting who regulates proceedings, and nonconformity as refusal to unite with an established church.

expand to see more

MOD'ERATOR, n. The person who presides over a meeting or assembly to preserve order and regulate proceedings.

NONCONFORM'ITY, n. Neglect or failure of conformity; refusal to unite with an established church.

CORONA'TION, n. The act or solemnity of crowning a sovereign.

CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who performs divine service in an army, a ship or a family.

Act 4:19 — "But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."

Modern Corruption

The Moderator who crowned Charles II and refused his bishopric.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy partisan reading of 1651 that treats every Resolutioner as a time-server. Douglas crowned a king, warned him to his face in the coronation sermon, led the party that compromised, and then declined the reward when it came and lost his pulpit for it. The historical record will not reduce to two parties of the faithful and the pliable.

The principle to recover is that honour to the magistrate and obedience to God are both commanded and that their order is fixed when they collide. Peter puts the honour unqualified — “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17) — and he had already settled the precedence before the council: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).

"“to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19) — the refused bishopric of 1662."
